addressed_problems.content: While the current study demonstrates that for MLP-based agents in both supervised behavioral cloning and deep reinforcement learning the IMP-identified mask contributes more to the lottery ticket effect than the preserved initial weights, the opposite pattern is observed for CNN-based agents on certain tasks such as Asterix and Space Invaders in MinAtar. The precise conditions—including architecture choice, task complexity, optimization algorithm, and sparsity level—under which the initial weight values become a dominant contributor to the ticket effect in reinforcement learning remain to be systematically characterized. Understanding this transition is important for guiding pruning strategies and initialization schemes across different RL settings.

The current study shows that the IMP-derived input-layer mask acts as a minimal task representation by pruning entire task-irrelevant input dimensions, yielding interpretable inductive biases in both low-dimensional control and high-dimensional visual tasks. However, it remains unresolved whether this representation-regularization interpretation generalizes to masks at intermediate and higher network layers. The extent to which deeper-layer masks encode minimal abstractions, and whether they can be similarly interpreted as compressing task-relevant features, is an open question. Addressing this could lead to more interpretable hidden representations and potentially sparser networks, as suggested by the possibility of pruning entire units of intermediate layers.

The paper establishes that agents trained via reinforcement learning require a larger number of parameters to maintain performance compared to agents trained via supervised behavioral cloning, indicating that the non-stationarity and exploration demands of RL increase the minimal size of winning tickets. However, the specific contributions of the three distinct RL-specific challenges—the exploration problem, within-training covariate shift (distribution shift), and the nature and quality of the credit-assignment signal—to this increased parameter requirement have not been isolated. Disentangling these factors is necessary to understand the fundamental constraints on sparsity in deep RL and to design RL-specific pruning algorithms that can match the pruning efficiency of supervised learning.

The current study uses global magnitude-based pruning and highlights the importance of initialization scales (e.g., Kaiming vs. Xavier) for discovering minimal input representations. However, systematic investigations of layer-specific pruning ratios, normalization schemes, and alternative initialization strategies are needed to identify sparser, more efficient, and more interpretable winning tickets in deep reinforcement learning. Additionally, pruning entire units (neurons) of intermediate layers—rather than individual weights—could improve the interpretability of hidden representations and may yield different lottery ticket effects. These methodological directions remain open for future research.

The empirical findings of this study demonstrate that iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) can uncover minimal task representations in deep reinforcement learning—for example, by identifying that only the pole angle and angular velocity are sufficient for the Cart-Pole task, or that only the angular velocities of the two links are needed for the Acrobot task. However, a theoretical account of why and when IMP discovers such minimal representations is lacking. Developing theoretical foundations to explain the emergence of task-relevant inductive biases through pruning, the role of initialization scales, and the conditions under which IMP yields minimal representations is an important open direction for future work.

The paper addresses how the "lottery ticket hypothesis" (existence of sparse sub-networks that can be trained to match dense-network performance) extends to reinforcement learning (RL) and what mechanisms produce winning tickets in RL. Prior work had established lottery tickets in supervised settings and provided initial evidence for tickets in RL, but left open how the distinctive aspects of RL—non-stationary data distributions caused by the agent’s evolving policy, the need for exploration, and a different credit-assignment signal—interact with iterative magnitude pruning (IMP). In supervised learning IMP operates on a static training dataset and often attributes success to either the binary mask (which connections survive) or the preserved initial weight values; in RL it is unclear whether small-magnitude weights at the end of training were nonetheless required during earlier exploration phases, or whether magnitude-based pruning of a policy distorts learning dynamics because weights can play different roles across learning stages. Moreover, practical application of IMP in RL raises additional methodological questions: how to disentangle the contributions of the binary mask, the preserved initial weights, and the layer-wise pruning ratios; whether IMP yields interpretable, minimal input representations in high- and low-dimensional observation spaces; and whether standard weight-initialization schemes introduce layer-dependent biases that systematically affect which units are pruned. These unresolved issues prevented a clear understanding of (a) whether winning tickets reliably exist across on-/off-policy RL algorithms and across visual and low-dimensional control tasks, (b) what component of a ticket (mask versus preserved initialization) carries the effective inductive bias in RL, and (c) whether and how IMP can be used as a tool to discover minimal, task-sufficient input representations in RL.

nodes.content: Understanding whether the inductive advantage of a winning ticket comes from structural sparsity (which inputs/hidden units are used) or from fortunate initial weight values is crucial for both theoretical interpretation and practical deployment of pruning techniques. Prior evidence in supervised image classification suggested a substantial role for initial weights in some settings, but it was unknown whether the same held in RL or in MLP agents trained on control tasks. Without establishing which component drives performance, it is unclear whether IMP primarily discovers a useful sparse architecture (mask) or merely preserves advantageous initializations that the optimizer exploits.

Architecture-specific differences (dense fully connected layers versus convolutional layers) may affect whether IMP discovers performance-preserving masks independent of the retained initial weight values. Prior work had not systematically compared the relative importance of mask vs. preserved initial weights across architectures in RL settings. If the preserved initial weights matter more for CNNs, then architectural choices and initialization schemes must be considered when interpreting tickets and when designing pruning strategies for vision-based RL agents.

In supervised learning, winning tickets were demonstrated on static datasets and for commonly used optimization procedures, giving rise to the hypothesis that overparameterization is not always necessary for final performance. In RL the data-generating distribution is non-stationary and coupled to the learned policy; furthermore, standard RL algorithms differ from supervised optimizers in objective, stability, and exploration requirements. Before this work it was unclear whether IMP would produce sparse, trainable sub-networks that preserve performance under these dynamic conditions, or whether the covariate shift and exploration needs of RL would prevent the discovery or utility of such tickets. The absence of broad empirical evidence across different RL algorithms and task types left open whether the lottery-ticket phenomenon generalizes beyond supervised settings and specific RL instantiations.

Practitioners and theorists need to know whether the extra difficulty of RL (exploration and evolving data distribution) materially increases the number of degrees of freedom required in a network relative to supervised learning on comparable predictive tasks. Prior analyses of lottery tickets in supervised settings do not separate the effects of non-stationarity and exploration. Without direct comparison to a supervised imitation (behavioral cloning) baseline, it remained unknown whether observed ticket size limits in RL stem from fundamental algorithmic differences (e.g., exploration) or from other confounding factors. This uncertainty impeded precise claims about how many parameters are necessary to handle the additional challenges of RL versus supervised learning.

The lottery-ticket effect conflates at least three factors—(i) which connections are retained (the binary mask), (ii) the original initial weight values that are preserved at retained locations, and (iii) layer-specific sparsity budgets introduced by global or layerwise pruning heuristics. Prior empirical studies often compared only the full IMP ticket to a random sparse reinitialization, leaving ambiguous which of these components primarily produces the performance gap. Without carefully designed counterfactuals that selectively break these components, it is impossible to attribute the source of the ticket effect and to draw mechanistic conclusions about why a given sparse sub-network succeeds.

For both interpretability and computational efficiency it is desirable to know whether pruning can reveal which observation dimensions are truly necessary to accomplish a control objective. Prior to this work it was unclear if IMP would merely remove redundant synapses while leaving all input dimensions effectively available, or whether it would systematically eliminate entire inputs to produce a minimal, actionable representation. This distinction matters because eliminating whole input channels enables input-compression and can reveal physical affordances of the task; absent such evidence, practitioners cannot reliably use IMP masks as inductive priors or for input-dimension selection.

IMP operates by ranking weight magnitudes globally (or across layers) and pruning the smallest; therefore, systematic differences in initial activation/weight scales across layers can lead IMP to target some layers preferentially for removal regardless of task relevance. Before this investigation it was not established whether commonly used initialization schemes introduce such a bias in RL/IMP pipelines, nor whether a simple rescaling heuristic can mitigate the bias and improve the reliability of discovering genuinely task-relevant input dimensions. Without addressing initialization-scale effects, reported masks may reflect initialization artifacts rather than meaningful minimal representations.

Iterative magnitude pruning (IMP), applied as training a network, pruning 20% of weights with smallest global magnitude, resetting the remaining weights to their initial values, and iterating, produces sparse networks (winning tickets) that achieve performance comparable to dense networks in multiple reinforcement-learning settings: on-policy Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and off-policy Deep Q-Network (DQN) optimization formulations, across high-dimensional visual navigation tasks (GridMaze with observations $o_t \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 10 \times 20}$), MinAtar environments (e.g., Freeway, SpaceInvaders, Breakout, Asterix) and ALE Atari benchmark environments (e.g., Breakout), continuous control tasks (PyBullet environments: HalfCheetah, Walker2D, Ant), and discrete low-dimensional control tasks (CartPole, Acrobot). The lottery-ticket phenomenon is observable and robustly reproducible across these RL settings.

metadata.narrative: The derivation of Conclusion 1 rests on empirical demonstrations across two RL algorithms and over ten distinct task environments. The primary load-bearing risk is P1: the limited training budget for Atari environments may produce spurious ticket effects that could vanish with longer training, which would narrow the scope of the conclusion by removing Atari-class tasks from the supported domain. However, H1 and H2 mitigate this risk substantially: H1's breadth across algorithms and tasks means that even if Atari results are excluded, the conclusion holds for all other settings; H2's best-checkpoint tracking reduces the chance that any ticket observation is a noise artifact in any setting. P1 thus only creates a risk of scope reduction, not collapse. Among the highlights, H1 is the most load-bearing: without the algorithm/task breadth, the conclusion would apply only to a narrow slice of RL. H2 is confirming but not essential given the consistent pattern across settings. The overall credibility is high because the core phenomenon—winning tickets exist in RL—is robustly shown across the majority of the tested settings regardless of the Atari uncertainty.

nodes.title: Iterative magnitude pruning produces winning tickets across on-policy and off-policy RL algorithms and diverse task modalities

nodes.content: For matched architectures on CartPole, Acrobot, and PyBullet continuous control tasks (HalfCheetah, Walker2D, Ant), networks trained via supervised behavioral cloning (student imitating a fixed expert policy, i.e., learning under a stationary data distribution) can be pruned to substantially higher sparsity levels before performance degrades than networks trained with reinforcement learning (Proximal Policy Optimization, PPO). Hence, solving the full RL problem (which entails exploration, within-training distributional shift, and a different credit-assignment signal) increases the minimal number of parameters required for successful learning in those tasks.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 attributes the larger minimal parameter requirement in RL to the additional challenges of exploration, distribution shift, and credit assignment. P2 argues that the observed gap may be simply a training budget effect: sparse RL agents may not have been trained to convergence, making them artificially appear to need more parameters. H3 provides a controlled experimental design that reduces many confounds, but it does not address the budget issue because both BC and RL used the same fixed step budgets. Therefore, P2 remains exposed: if the budget is insufficient for RL at high sparsity, the conclusion's causal attribution is undermined. No highlight directly preempts the budget concern; H3 only ensures that the comparison is otherwise clean. The composite risk is that the quantitative sparsity thresholds and the qualitative claim that RL requires more parameters could both be artifacts of insufficient training, leaving the conclusion moderately supported at best.

nodes.title: Supervised behavioural cloning yields smaller minimal tickets than reinforcement learning

nodes.content: A set of controlled counterfactual baselines was defined and used to disentangle components of the winning ticket obtained via iterative magnitude pruning (IMP): (a) mask/weights (retain both the IMP-derived binary mask and the preserved initial weight values), (b) mask/permuted (retain the IMP-derived mask and layer-wise pruning ratios but permute the preserved initial weight values among themselves within each layer), (c) permuted/permuted (permute both the binary mask and the preserved initial weight values while retaining layer-wise pruning ratios), and (d) random/re-init (sample random binary masks for each layer without preserving layer-wise pruning ratios and re-initialize all weights). These baselines enable separating the contribution of the precise binary mask, the preserved initial weight values, and the layer-wise pruning ratios to the overall ticket effect.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 3 claims that the defined baselines enable separation of mask, weight initialization, and pruning ratio contributions. P3 identifies a limitation in the mask/permuted baseline: preserving layer-wise weight statistics may retain some initialization benefits, so the isolation of initialization contribution is incomplete. This weakens the claim that the baselines fully separate these components. H4 (the hierarchical design) provides a principled framework that is sound as a logical decomposition, but the empirical inference still depends on the adequacy of each specific comparison. The risk identified by P3 is that the mask/permuted baseline may not be a perfect counterfactual for "no initialization advantage", but the hierarchical structure still allows for relative comparisons (e.g., the gap between mask/weights and mask/permuted should be interpreted as an upper bound on the initialization contribution, not a precise estimate). The overall credibility is moderate: the baselines are useful and structurally sound, but their ability to fully disentangle the contributions is not guaranteed. No highlight fully addresses the P3 concern; H4 provides the logical justification but does not empirically close the gap.

nodes.title: Methodological baselines to disentangle mask, weight initialization, and layer-wise pruning ratio

nodes.content: Iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) frequently prunes entire input units (columns of the first linear layer) thereby eliminating whole observation dimensions that are not task-relevant; this effect occurs in high-dimensional visual tasks (GridMaze with observations $o_t \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 10 \times 20}$) and in low-dimensional control tasks (CartPole, Acrobot, and PyBullet continuous control). The resulting IMP input-layer mask provides a compressed, interpretable, task-sufficient representation: training a new dense network using only the input dimensions retained by the IMP mask attains learning speed and final performance comparable to training on the full observation space. The preserved input features encode physically meaningful quantities (e.g., for GridMaze: proximity of patrolling enemy and coin/poison locations; for CartPole: pole angle and pole angular velocity; for Acrobot: angular velocities of the two links) and thus constitute minimal task representations discovered by IMP.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 5 makes two subclaims: (a) that IMP produces a task-sufficient input representation and (b) that this representation is minimal. H7 and H8 strongly support (a): the transfer experiment shows sufficiency, and interpretability confirms that pruned dimensions are task-irrelevant. P7 and P8 challenge (b): the lack of a random subset baseline means sufficiency could be trivial, and no evidence is provided that no smaller subset suffices. P7 is the dominant risk: the term "minimal" in the conclusion's title overstates what is demonstrated; the conclusion body itself uses "minimal" but also "compressed" and "task-sufficient", so the claim is ambiguous. H8 partially addresses the concern that the mask selection is arbitrary, by showing interpretable structure. However, the absence of a random subset baseline (P8) remains a significant gap: the sufficiency might not be special to the IMP mask. The overall credibility is moderate; the sufficiency claim is well-supported, but the minimality claim lacks empirical backing, reducing confidence in the stronger interpretation.

nodes.title: IMP yields task-sufficient input representations; input masks transfer to dense training

nodes.content: The scale induced by common initialization heuristics causes a layer-dependent pruning bias: Kaiming-style initializations produce smaller initial weight magnitudes in layers with large input dimensionality, which makes those layers more susceptible to being pruned by global-magnitude iterative magnitude pruning (IMP); Xavier-type initializations avoid this specific bias. In experiments with CartPole and Acrobot, downscaling the Kaiming initialization of the input layer by a factor of ten (i.e., multiplying input-layer initial weights by 0.1) accelerates and stabilizes the discovery of minimal task-relevant input dimensions by IMP, while other rescaling factors (e.g., 0.01, 0.5, 1.0) either slow the separation or cause overly aggressive pruning.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 6 claims both (a) that initialization scale biases pruning in a layer-dependent way and (b) that rescaled Kaiming input initialization (factor 0.1) robustly promotes discovery of minimal representations. H9 provides strong evidence for (a) by comparing Kaiming and Xavier initializations, showing the bias is initialization-induced. For (b), P9 and P10 identify that the rescaling heuristic is tested on only two low-dimensional tasks and without a systematic factor sweep, so the claim that it robustly promotes discovery is not empirically grounded beyond those specific settings. The bias detection (a) is a highlight of the paper and is well-supported. The rescaling recommendation (b) remains largely heuristic with limited support. The two subclaims have very different strengths: (a) is high-credibility, (b) is low. Because the conclusion as a whole bundles them, the overall prior probability is moderate-to-low, reflecting that the practical recommendation is not robustly validated. No highlight addresses the limitations of the rescaling heuristic beyond the two tasks.

nodes.title: Layer-specific initialization scale biases pruning; input-layer rescaling promotes robust discovery in low-dimensional control

nodes.content: For multilayer perceptron (MLP) agents in supervised behavioral cloning (on CartPole, Acrobot, and PyBullet continuous control tasks) and reinforcement-learning experiments (on the same tasks via Proximal Policy Optimization, and on GridMaze visual navigation via Deep Q-Network, and on MinAtar environments via behavioral cloning and DQN), the majority of the lottery-ticket effect is explained by the IMP-derived binary mask (which connections survive) rather than by the preserved initial weight values. Specifically, training performance of mask/weights tickets (retaining both IMP mask and preserved initial weights) and mask/permuted tickets (retaining IMP mask but permuting preserved initial weight values within each layer) is similar, whereas distorting or re-sampling the mask (permuted/permuted, which permutes both mask and weights, or random/re-init, which samples random masks and re-initializes weights) substantially degrades performance at comparable sparsity levels.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4a asserts that the IMP-derived mask is the principal contributor to the ticket effect for MLP agents. P4 notes that the mask/permuted baseline may not fully eliminate initialization effects because it retains weight distribution statistics, potentially overstating the mask's role. However, H5 demonstrates that the mask's dominance is replicated across six or more diverse experimental conditions (behavioral cloning and RL on multiple tasks), each with multiple seeds. Even under a conservative adjustment for the baseline limitation, the consistent small gap between mask/weights and mask/permuted across all these conditions strongly indicates the mask as the primary factor. The quantitative magnitude of the mask contribution is robustly established, though the possibility of a non-zero weight contribution remains. P4 is thus a refinement risk, not a collapse risk. H5 is the primary load-bearing support, and H4 (the baseline hierarchy, though assigned to conclusion 3) provides the experimental framework that makes the claim interpretable. The cumulative evidence pushes the prior probability above the premise's own estimated credibility because the replication across conditions provides strong corroboration even if each individual measurement is imperfect.

nodes.title: IMP-derived mask is the principal contributor to the ticket effect for MLP-based agents

nodes.content: For convolutional neural network (CNN) based agents (with architecture: convolutional layers with 16 filters of size 3, followed by fully connected layers of 128 and 64 units) trained on MinAtar environments (Freeway, SpaceInvaders, Breakout, Asterix) in both behavioral cloning and DQN experiments, the preserved initial weight values contribute more to the lottery-ticket effect than for MLP agents: the gap between mask/weights and mask/permuted baselines is larger for certain MinAtar games (e.g., Asterix, SpaceInvaders), indicating that initialization information is more important for those convolutional architectures and tasks.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4b claims that preserved initial weights play a larger role for CNN-based agents than for MLP-based agents. P5 limits the empirical basis to a single CNN architecture on four MinAtar games, leaving generalization to other CNN variants and visual RL tasks untested. P6 raises a more fundamental concern: the mask/permuted baseline may disproportionately damage CNN performance because permuting convolutional filters disrupts spatial structure, inflating the apparent weight contribution. H6 shows a clean comparison between MLP and CNN on the same tasks, establishing that a difference exists in this controlled setting. However, P5 and P6 jointly limit the conclusion to the tested architecture and tasks, and the baseline artifact could partly explain the gap. The weakest link is P6: if the mask/permuted baseline is architecturally destructive for CNNs, then even the controlled comparison does not separate the true weight contribution from the baseline destructiveness. No highlight directly insulates against this risk. The overall credibility is low; the claim is plausible but not convincingly supported beyond the specific shallow-CNN-on-MinAtar configuration.

nodes.title: Weight initialization plays a larger role for CNN-based agents than for MLP agents

nodes.content:
In the evaluation of winning tickets in reinforcement learning via iterative magnitude pruning (IMP; train → prune 20% of global smallest-magnitude weights → reset remaining weights to their initial values → repeat), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agents on ALE Atari benchmark environments (e.g., Breakout) are trained for only 2.5 million environment frames per IMP iteration, which is substantially less than the tens of millions of frames typically used for convergence in Atari. Therefore, the observed parity between the sparse IMP-derived network and the dense network at certain sparsity levels may be an artifact of insufficient training rather than evidence that the sparse sub-network can be trained to match the dense network's asymptotic performance.
      Table 9 (Atari PPO hyperparameters)

metadata.failure_mode: If the training budget for Atari environments is insufficient (true), then the observed comparable performance of sparse networks may disappear if training were extended to convergence. In that case, the conclusion that winning tickets exist in Atari-class tasks (a subset of the tasks listed in the conclusion) would be invalidated. The conclusion's scope would be narrowed to non-Atari tasks (visual navigation, MinAtar, low-dimensional control). The intermediate step that fails is the measurement step: the observed returns do not reliably indicate asymptotic policy quality, because training was truncated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The training budget per IMP iteration (2.5M frames) is an order of magnitude smaller than standard Atari training protocols (typically 50M frames). The paper itself acknowledges "Due to computational considerations we limit each individual IMP iteration for the ATARI environments to 2.5 million frames." This is a pragmatic compromise, but it introduces a systematic risk that the ticket effect in Atari may reflect incomplete training rather than true sparsity robustness. The field standard for Atari convergence uses far more frames, and the paper does not check whether results change with longer training. The claim of ticket existence relies on the measured performance at these budgets accurately reflecting the asymptotic performance of sparse sub-networks.

nodes.title: Limited Atari training budget may produce spurious tickets

nodes.content: In the comparison between behavioral cloning (BC) and reinforcement learning (RL) on matched tasks (CartPole, Acrobot, PyBullet continuous control), both BC and RL agents are trained for a pre-calibrated number of environment steps that was determined for the dense network. For RL agents, the necessary number of training steps may increase as the network becomes sparser because exploration becomes more difficult; therefore, the earlier performance degradation of RL at higher sparsity levels could reflect insufficient training budget rather than a fundamentally larger minimal parameter requirement for solving the RL problem.

metadata.failure_mode: If the weak point is true (sparse RL agents need more training steps than given), then the observed earlier performance degradation of RL agents at high sparsity levels would be a training-budget artifact, not evidence of a larger minimal parameter requirement. Consequently, the conclusion that "solving the full RL problem increases the minimal number of parameters required for successful learning" would be unsupported by this experiment; the gap could potentially vanish with extended training. The quantitative sparsity thresholds at which performance drops would shift or disappear.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper uses pre-calibrated generous training steps, but these are calibrated for dense networks. For sparse networks in RL, the exploration-exploitation dynamics may converge more slowly, requiring more interaction to reach the same performance level. The paper does not test whether extending training for sparse RL agents closes the gap with BC agents. Without such a test, the conclusion that RL inherently requires more parameters conflates the RL-specific challenges with a training budget confound. The causal attribution to exploration/distribution shift/credit-assignment signal is weakened because a simpler alternative explanation exists: insufficient training steps.

nodes.title: Insufficient training for sparse RL agents may cause apparent larger parameter requirement

nodes.content: In the mask/permuted baseline used to isolate the contribution of preserved initial weight values to the lottery ticket effect, the weights surviving in each layer after iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) are randomly permuted among themselves, preserving the layer-wise empirical mean, variance, and higher moments of the retained weight distribution. Consequently, any training benefit that depends on the statistical properties (e.g., scale, variance) of the preserved weight distribution, rather than on the specific assignment of weight values to unit connections, is retained in this baseline, so the baseline does not fully eliminate the contribution of the weight initialization to the ticket effect.

metadata.failure_mode: If the weak point is true (distributional properties of the initial weights are retained and contribute to training), then the observed virtual absence of a gap between mask/weights and mask/permuted does not prove that weight initialization is unimportant; it only proves that the specific assignment of weight to unit positions does not matter. The conclusion that the mask is the principal contributor (Conclusion 4a) would be over-stated, as a partially preserved initialization effect could be conflated with the mask's contribution. The effective attribution of the ticket effect to the mask would be inflated.
metadata.weakness_reason: Permuting weights within a layer destroys the specific connectivity but preserves the histogram of weight values (mean, variance, and higher moments). Many properties of weight initialization known to affect training (e.g., variance that balances signal propagation, spectral properties of the weight matrix) depend only on the overall distribution, not on which specific unit gets which weight. Therefore, the mask/permuted baseline may still retain these distributional benefits, leading to an underestimate of the contribution of initial weight values to the ticket effect. The paper interprets the small gap between mask/weights and mask/permuted as evidence that the mask dominates, but this interpretation relies on the assumption that permuting eliminates all initialization-related advantage, which is questionable.

nodes.title: Mask/permuted baseline retains initialization statistics, limiting separation

nodes.content: In the mask/permuted baseline used to isolate the contribution of preserved initial weight values to the lottery ticket effect, the weights surviving in each layer after iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) are randomly permuted among themselves, preserving the layer-wise empirical mean, variance, and higher moments of the retained weight distribution. Consequently, any training benefit that depends on the statistical properties (e.g., scale, variance) of the preserved weight distribution, rather than on the specific assignment of weight values to unit connections, is retained in this baseline, so the baseline does not fully eliminate the contribution of the weight initialization to the ticket effect.

metadata.failure_mode: If the baseline retains some initialization effects, then the performance of mask/permuted would be artificially high, making the mask's apparent contribution appear larger than its true standalone contribution. The conclusion that the mask is the principal contributor could be quantitatively shifted: the mask's share of the total ticket effect would be overestimated. However, because the gap is small to begin with, even a moderate correction would still leave the mask as a major contributor, so the failure mode is a quantitative refinement, not a structural collapse. The qualitative direction (mask matters more than weights) is likely robust, but the "principal" claim may be weakened.
metadata.weakness_reason: Same underlying reasoning as P3. For MLP agents, the gap between mask/weights and mask/permuted is small, but if the mask/permuted baseline retains initialization statistics that help training, the mask is not as dominant as the raw gap suggests. The paper claims "the majority of the lottery ticket effect is explained by the IMP-derived binary mask." Even with a conservative correction, the mask may still be the primary factor, but the quantitative strength of the claim is reduced.

nodes.title: Same baseline limitation affects mask-dominance claim for MLP

nodes.content: In experiments using a single convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture (convolutional layers: 16 filters of size 3, followed by fully connected layers of 128 and 64 units) on four MinAtar environments (Freeway, SpaceInvaders, Breakout, Asterix), preserved initial weights contribute more for CNN agents than for MLP agents. However, the generalizability to other CNN designs (e.g., deeper Atari-style CNNs, architectures with batch normalization or pooling, different filter sizes) and to other visual reinforcement learning tasks is untested; therefore, the observed larger contribution of weight initialization for CNN-based agents may not hold beyond the tested configuration.

metadata.failure_mode: If the generalizability is limited (true), the conclusion that "weight initialization plays a larger role for CNN-based agents" would be overgeneralized. The conclusion would not be valid for the full range of CNN architectures and visual RL tasks that practitioners use; it would only apply to the specific shallow CNN on MinAtar. The failure mode is a scope reduction: the claim as stated (without qualification) is premature.
metadata.weakness_reason: The MinAtar environments use low-resolution (10x10) observations and the CNN is shallow (one convolutional layer of 16 3x3 filters); this is far from the deeper CNNs commonly used in Atari (e.g., Nature DQN CNN: 3 convolutional layers, 32-64-64 filters). The paper does not test whether the larger role of weights holds for deeper CNNs, different observation sizes, or different training algorithms (e.g., PPO with CNNs on Atari). Without such evidence, the claim is narrowly scoped.

nodes.title: Limited CNN architecture and task coverage for weight-importance claim

nodes.content: In the mask/permuted baseline as applied to convolutional layers, permuting the weights within each convolutional layer disrupts the spatial arrangement of filter coefficients. For convolutional layers, the spatial structure of weights is crucial, as learned filters (e.g., edge detectors) depend on the relative positions of weights. Therefore, permuting weights within a convolutional layer may degrade performance more severely than permuting within a fully connected layer for reasons unrelated to the value of the particular initial weight values, and the resulting larger gap between mask/weights and mask/permuted for CNN agents may partly reflect this architectural disruption rather than a genuinely larger contribution of the preserved weight initialization.

metadata.failure_mode: If this weak point is true, then the larger gap between mask/weights and mask/permuted for CNN agents is not a clean measure of the initialization contribution; it partly reflects the architectural destructiveness of the permutation operation. Consequently, the claim that "preserved initial weights contribute more for CNN-based agents" could be an artifact of a flawed baseline rather than a genuine architectural difference. The quantitative gap would be overestimated, possibly to the point where the conclusion that weights matter more for CNNs is unsupported when using an appropriate baseline (e.g., swapping the entire set of weights of one layer with another layer's weights to preserve spatial structure).
metadata.weakness_reason: In fully connected layers, each weight connects an input unit to an output unit, and permuting the location of weights within the layer preserves the overall connectivity pattern at the individual unit level (each output unit still receives the same distribution of incoming weights). In a convolutional layer, each weight's position defines which spatial location of the input it operates on (e.g., the 3x3 kernel position). Permuting within the convolutional layer destroys this spatial organization, likely degrading the layer's representational power far more than the corresponding permutation in a fully connected layer. Thus, the mask/permuted baseline is not an equivalent counterfactual across architectures; the gap for CNNs may be artificially inflated.

nodes.title: Permutation disrupts CNN filter structure, inflating weight contribution

nodes.content: Training a new dense network on only the input dimensions retained by the iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) mask achieves performance comparable to training on the full observation. However, no comparison to a random subset of input dimensions of the same size is made, and no demonstration that no smaller subset (either from a different pruning procedure or a subset of the IMP-retained dimensions) would suffice is provided. Therefore, the claim that the IMP mask provides the smallest possible sufficient representation is not supported; the evidence only demonstrates sufficiency, not minimality.

metadata.failure_mode: If the weak point is true (no evidence for minimality), then the conclusion's use of "minimal" is misleading. The conclusion should be that IMP produces a sufficient task representation, not necessarily minimal. Readers may incorrectly infer that IMP discovers the sparsest possible input representation. The failure is a quantitative overstatement; the actual supported claim (sufficiency) is intact, but the additional inference of optimality is unsupported.
metadata.weakness_reason: The term "minimal" carries a specific meaning: that the identified subset of input dimensions is the smallest possible set that still allows successful task performance. To support this, one would need to search for smaller subsets (e.g., via systematic ablation, optimization, or exhaustive enumeration) and show that none works. The paper only shows that the IMP-retained subset works; it does not rule out the possibility that an even smaller subset (perhaps found by a different pruning method or by manual inspection) also works. The claim's strength goes beyond the evidence.

nodes.title: No evidence that IMP mask is minimal (smallest sufficient subset)

nodes.content: A dense network trained on only the input dimensions retained by the iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) mask (for both the visual navigation task and low-dimensional control tasks) is not compared to a dense network trained on an equally sized random subset of input dimensions. Without such a baseline, it is unclear whether the IMP mask's selection of input dimensions is truly task-sufficient because it retains the most relevant features, or whether any random subset of the same cardinality would also yield comparable performance due to abundant task-relevant information across many dimensions.

metadata.failure_mode: If a random subset of the same size also suffices, then the IMP mask's specific selection of input dimensions is not uniquely responsible for the preserved performance; the performance could be achieved by any subset of that size. The claim that the mask provides a "task-sufficient representation" would remain true (the subset works), but the additional connotation that the mask's specific pattern of surviving dimensions is important would be weakened. The interpretability analysis would still suggest meaningful pruning, but the control experiment would not distinguish between a well-chosen set and a random set of the same size.
metadata.weakness_reason: The transfer experiment shows that the IMP-retained subset works, but it does not control for the cardinality effect. If the original observation space contains many redundant dimensions, any random subset of the same size might also suffice. Therefore, the specific structure of the IMP mask may not be necessary; the fact that a random subset also works would weaken the claim that the mask has discovered a structurally meaningful minimal representation. The paper's interpretability analysis (H8) provides qualitative evidence that the pruned dimensions are irrelevant, which partially mitigates this concern, but the quantitative baseline is missing.

nodes.title: Transfer experiment lacks random input subset baseline

nodes.content: Multiplying Kaiming initialization weights of the input layer by a factor of 0.1 to promote robust discovery of minimal input representations by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) is tested only on two low-dimensional control tasks: CartPole (4 input dimensions) and Acrobot (6 input dimensions). The effectiveness and robustness of this rescaling heuristic for higher-dimensional input tasks (e.g., PyBullet continuous control with 22–28 dimensions, or visual navigation with 1200 dimensions) is not demonstrated; therefore, the claim that input-layer rescaling 'promotes robust discovery' is unsupported beyond the studied low-dimensional settings.

metadata.failure_mode: If the weak point is true (heuristic does not generalize), then the conclusion that input-layer rescaling promotes robust discovery would be false for most practical RL settings with higher-dimensional inputs. The claim would only be valid for low-dimensional control tasks like CartPole and Acrobot. The failure reduces the scope of the conclusion dramatically.
metadata.weakness_reason: The claim that a specific rescaling factor (0.1) robustly promotes discovery is based on a very narrow empirical basis. The tasks tested have very low input dimensionality (4 and 6), where the layer-specific pruning bias might behave differently than in higher-dimensional settings (e.g., 1200 input channels in the visual navigation task). The paper does not test whether the same rescaling factor works for the PyBullet tasks or the visual navigation task, which were studied in earlier sections. Without such tests, the generality of the heuristic is unknown.

nodes.title: Rescaling heuristic tested only on two low-dimensional tasks

nodes.content: In the investigation of input-layer rescaling to mitigate initialization bias in iterative magnitude pruning (IMP), the rescaling factor of 0.1 is applied heuristically to the Kaiming initialization of the input layer. A systematic sweep across possible factors is not performed to determine the optimal value or to assess whether the robustness of the discovery is sensitive to the exact factor. The choice of 0.1 is justified only by comparing a few ad-hoc values (0.01, 0.5, 1.0) on CartPole and Acrobot, which is insufficient to support a general recommendation for this specific factor.

metadata.failure_mode: If the weak point is true (the optimal factor is task-dependent or sensitive), then the recommendation of 0.1 may not generalize even to CartPole and Acrobot with different random seeds or architecture variations. The claim that the rescaling "promotes robust discovery" would be unsupported; the observed success could be a coincidence. The practical utility of the heuristic is undermined.
metadata.weakness_reason: The selection of 0.1 is based on a sparse comparison of four values (0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0). This is not a proper hyperparameter search; the paper does not report the results of the unsystematic comparisons (e.g., did they try 0.05? 0.2?). The recommendation appears to be an ad-hoc heuristic. If the goal is to promote robust discovery, one would need to demonstrate that the factor works reliably across multiple seeds and tasks, and ideally provide a principled rule (e.g., based on input dimensionality) rather than a fixed value. The lack of a sweep means the result could be fragile to small changes in the factor or random seed.

nodes.title: No systematic sweep of rescaling factor

nodes.content: The paper demonstrates winning tickets (sub-networks achieving comparable performance to the dense network when trained) across multiple reinforcement learning settings including two fundamentally different optimization families—on-policy (Proximal Policy Optimization, PPO) and off-policy (Deep Q-Network, DQN)—and across a diverse set of tasks: high-dimensional visual navigation in a grid maze ($o_t \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 10 \times 20}$), MinAtar tasks (Freeway, SpaceInvaders, Breakout, Asterix), ALE Atari games (e.g., Breakout, Pong), and low-dimensional continuous/discrete control (PyBullet environments: HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2D, Ant; CartPole; Acrobot). This broad empirical coverage across algorithms and task modalities means that the lottery ticket phenomenon in RL is not specific to a narrow set of conditions.

metadata.credit: The conclusion's central claim—that winning tickets are observable and robustly reproducible in RL—is directly supported by the breadth of tested settings. Without this coverage, one could argue that the ticket phenomenon only appears under specific conditions (e.g., only in on-policy algorithms or only in continuous control). The wide algorithm (PPO, DQN) and task (visual, discrete, continuous) coverage preempts that alternative explanation and underwrites the generalization layer of the conclusion. The scope of credit is full underwriting of the qualitative existence claim across the tested space.

nodes.title: Wide empirical coverage across algorithms and tasks

nodes.content: For each iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) iteration, the paper tracks the best-performing network checkpoint (in terms of average return over evaluation episodes) during training rather than the final network after the prescribed number of training steps. This reduces the influence of unstable training dynamics and noisy convergence that are common in RL, ensuring that the reported ticket performance represents the actual capability of the sparse sub-network rather than a collapse at the end of training.

metadata.credit: In RL, the final checkpoint can be poor due to policy collapse or exploration noise even if the agent reached a good policy earlier. By using the best checkpoint, the paper avoids the failure mode where a ticket is incorrectly judged as non-existent because of a bad final evaluation. This methodological choice strengthens the measurement of the ticket effect, making it less likely that the observed parity with dense networks is an artifact of noise. It underwrites the reliability of each individual ticket observation, which aggregates to higher confidence in the overall existence claim.

nodes.title: Best-performance tracking reduces noise in ticket measurement

nodes.content: The comparison between behavioral cloning (BC) and reinforcement learning (RL) is performed with matched network architectures (same number of layers and units), matched task environments (CartPole, Acrobot, PyBullet), and matched hyperparameters (learning rate, optimizer, network size) except for the training data source (static expert demonstrations for BC versus agent-collected experience for RL) and the loss function (KL divergence for BC versus policy gradient for RL). This controlled design reduces the number of confounding factors and strengthens the attribution of any sparsity-level difference to the distinctive demands of RL (exploration, non-stationarity, credit-assignment signal).

metadata.credit: Without matched architectures and hyperparameters, a difference in sparsity tolerance between BC and RL could be attributed to different network capacities, optimization settings, or task definitions. By holding these factors constant, the controlled comparison preempts these alternative explanations and supports the causal attribution of the sparsity gap to the RL-specific challenges. The layer of credibility underwritten is the attribution of the effect to the RL problem formulation. The scope of credit is that the qualitative direction (RL requires more parameters) is credibly linked to the RL difficulties, though the quantitative magnitude may still be affected by training budget (P2).

nodes.title: Controlled comparison of BC and RL minimizes confounds

nodes.content: The paper introduces a hierarchical set of four baseline configurations for lottery ticket analysis: (1) mask/weights—retain both IMP-derived binary mask and the preserved initial weights; (2) mask/permuted—retain mask but layer-wise permute the remaining weights; (3) permuted/permuted—layer-wise permute both mask and weights, retaining only layer-wise pruning ratios; (4) random/re-init—random binary mask and re-initialized weights. This hierarchy allows systematic decomposition of the contributions of the binary mask, the preserved initial weight values, and the layer-wise pruning ratio to the ticket effect, providing substantially more discrimination than the typical comparison between full ticket and random sparse network alone.

metadata.credit: The baseline hierarchy is a methodological strength that goes well beyond the standard practice in RL lottery ticket research (which only compared full ticket to random sparse). It enables the paper to ask which component of the ticket is responsible for the effect. Without this design, conclusions 4a and 4b would lack the necessary experimental controls to attribute the effect to mask vs. weights vs. pruning ratio. The hierarchy preempts the failure mode where practitioners incorrectly attribute the ticket effect to a single component when multiple factors are at play. The scope of credit is the full underwritings of the decompositional logic; it makes the subsequent attributions substantially more credible than they would be with a two-condition design.

nodes.title: Hierarchical baseline set allows principled decomposition

nodes.content: The finding that the IMP-derived binary mask is the principal contributor to the ticket effect (with preserved initial weights playing a much smaller role) is replicated across more than six separate experimental conditions: behavioral cloning on CartPole, Acrobot, and PyBullet (three tasks, Fig 3), and reinforcement learning on CartPole, Acrobot, GridMaze, PyBullet, and ATARI (five additional settings, Fig 4), each with multiple independent seeds. This consistent pattern across learning paradigms (supervised and RL) and across continuous and discrete control and visual tasks makes it unlikely that the mask-dominance is an artifact of a specific environment or algorithm.

metadata.credit: The robustness of the mask-dominance claim is demonstrated through repeated empirical replication across diverse tasks and learning paradigms. This replication guards against the failure mode where the result is driven by a specific environment's properties or by an idiosyncratic interaction between architecture and task. Each replication provides independent evidence that the mask carries the inductive bias. The layer underwritten is the qualitative direction and the generality of the mask-dominance across the tested regimes. The scope of credit is that even if the baseline limitation (P4) reduces the quantitative precision, the qualitative claim is well-supported by the consistency of the pattern.

nodes.title: Mask dominance replicated across many conditions

nodes.content: The comparison between MLP and CNN agents is conducted on the same set of MinAtar environments (Freeway, SpaceInvaders, Breakout, Asterix) with the same training algorithm (distillation from an expert value function), network size (matching the number of parameters approximately), and evaluation protocol. This controlled design isolates the effect of architecture (fully connected vs convolutional layers) on the relative contributions of mask and preserved initial weights, allowing the conclusion that weight initialization plays a larger role for CNNs to be attributed to architectural differences rather than to task-specific factors.

metadata.credit: Without matched environments and training protocols, a difference between CNN and MLP behavior could be caused by different tasks or training setups rather than architecture per se. The controlled comparison preempts that alternative explanation and supports the architectural attribution. The layer of credibility underwritten is the qualitative attribution to architecture (i.e., that CNNs differ from MLPs). The scope of credit is limited to the tested architecture and tasks (P5), but within that scope the comparison is clean.

nodes.title: Controlled architecture comparison on MinAtar isolates effect

nodes.content: For both the visual navigation task (object-map encoding, $o_t \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 10 \times 20}$) and low-dimensional control tasks (CartPole, Acrobot), the paper trains a new dense network from scratch using only the input dimensions (pixels or state variables) retained by the IMP mask after moderate sparsity (approximately 10% remaining weights). The dense network trained on this reduced input achieves performance curves (learning speed and final return) comparable to a dense network trained on the full observation space, as shown in Fig 5 (bottom right) and Fig 8 (bottom). This validates that the IMP mask itself encodes a sufficient input representation, independent of the specific sparse weights of the pruned network.

metadata.credit: The transfer experiment directly demonstrates that the mask (the set of surviving input dimensions) carries useful information for learning from scratch, not just within the specific pruned network's weight dynamics. This rules out the alternative explanation that the pruned network's performance depends on the preserved weight initialization across all layers interacting with the input mask. By isolating the input layer mask as a sufficient observation selection, the experiment underwrites the claim that IMP can compress the observation space. The layer of credibility is the sufficiency of the mask for learning; the scope of credit is full for sufficiency, but not for minimality (P7).

nodes.title: Transfer experiment validates sufficiency of IMP input mask

nodes.content: Visual inspection of the input layer masks reveals that the pruned input dimensions correspond to physically interpretable and task-irrelevant features across multiple tasks: in the visual navigation task, all pixels corresponding to enemy patrol areas that the agent cannot reach are pruned (Fig 5, left); in Freeway, pixels encoding the slowest-moving car (which does not require immediate reaction) are preferentially pruned; in SpaceInvaders, enemy bullet pixels more than one step away from the agent are pruned; in Breakout, the bottom row of the ball channel (which appears only when the ball has left the display and the episode terminates) is pruned; in CartPole, the cart position and velocity dimensions are pruned (Fig 8, top); in Acrobot, the sine and cosine of the two joint angles are pruned, leaving only angular velocities (Fig 8, middle). This interpretability shows that IMP captures meaningful task structure rather than arbitrary sparsity.

metadata.credit: The qualitative interpretability of the pruned dimensions provides corroborating evidence that IMP is not just selecting input dimensions arbitrarily but is identifying features that are causally irrelevant to the task. This preempts the alternative explanation (raised by P8) that sufficiency could occur with any random subset; the interpretable pattern shows that the pruned dimensions are specifically the non-informative ones, while the retained ones are the actionable ones. The layer of credibility is the mechanism: IMP identifies task-relevant structure. The scope of credit is that the mask selection is meaningful, even if the minimality claim (P7) is not proven.

nodes.title: Interpretable pruning patterns reveal genuine task-relevant compression

nodes.content: The paper demonstrates that Kaiming weight initialization produces systematically smaller initial weights in layers with larger input dimensionality, which biases global magnitude pruning to preferentially prune those layers. This bias is shown by comparing the cumulative input-layer weight magnitudes of agents trained with Kaiming initialization versus Xavier initialization: under Xavier initialization, the input layer weights are not disproportionately pruned, and the minimal input dimensions (cart position/velocity for CartPole, angular positions for Acrobot) are not separated from task-relevant dimensions (pole angle/angular velocity for CartPole, angular velocities for Acrobot) as cleanly (Fig 8, top rows, right column). This controlled comparison supports the claim that the pruning bias is initialization-induced rather than inherent to the reward structure.

metadata.credit: The comparison between Kaiming and Xavier initializations isolates the effect of the initialization scale on the layer-specific pruning behavior. Without this comparison, one could attribute the preferential pruning of input dimensions to the reward structure or task relevance rather than to an initialization artifact. By showing that Xavier (which does not have the same scale dependence on input dimensionality) does not produce the same pattern, the paper provides strong evidence for a causal mechanism linking initialization scale to pruning bias. This underwrites the claim that the bias is initialization-induced. The scope of credit is full for the existence of the bias and its mechanism; the rescaling recommendation (factor 0.1) is supported only as a proof-of-concept for the two low-dimensional tasks (P9, P10).

nodes.title: Controlled initialization comparison identifies pruning bias mechanism

steps.reasoning: Start from the upstream established baseline framework (conclusion 3): the mask/weights, mask/permuted, permuted/permuted, and random/re-init baselines are available and treated as known counterfactuals for attribution of ticket components.

Describe the experimental comparison for multilayer perceptron, abbreviated MLP, agents in supervised behavioral cloning: apply IMP to MLP student networks trained to imitate expert policies, and for each sparsity level evaluate the performance of the mask/weights ticket, the mask/permuted baseline (where the preserved weights are layer-wise permuted), and the permuted/permuted and random/re-init baselines.
Fig. 3

Report the empirical observation for MLP agents in behavioral cloning: the performance gap between the mask/weights ticket and the mask/permuted baseline is small (the red and green curves in the authors' plots overlap substantially), indicating that permuting preserved initial weights while keeping the IMP mask intact does not substantially reduce performance.
Fig. 3

Report the complementary empirical observation: distorting the IMP-derived mask (the permuted/permuted baseline) or replacing it with random masks and re-initialized weights (random/re-init) substantially degrades performance at comparable sparsity levels (the green versus blue/yellow curves show a marked gap), indicating that altering the mask has a larger negative effect than permuting preserved weight values.
Fig. 3

Extend the observation to reinforcement-learning MLP agents: in both on-policy (PPO) and off-policy (DQN) MLP-based experiments the same pattern holds — preserving the mask allows pruning to higher sparsity than when the mask is distorted, and permuting preserved weights while keeping the mask intact results in small performance loss — indicating that the mask is the primary carrier of ticket information for MLP agents in both supervised and RL settings.
Fig. 4

Conclude from these controlled counterfactual results that, for MLP-based agents in the experiments conducted, the majority of the lottery-ticket effect is explained by the IMP-derived binary mask (which connections survive) rather than by the preserved initial weight values; this is the interpretation the authors give based on the small mask/weights vs. mask/permuted gap and the large performance decline when the mask is distorted or randomized.

Start from the upstream baseline framework (conclusion 3) treated as known: the four baselines (mask/weights, mask/permuted, permuted/permuted, random/re-init) enable isolating mask and weight-initialization effects.

Describe the experimental comparison performed for convolutional neural network, abbreviated CNN, agents: the authors ran analogous baseline experiments for CNN-based agents (value estimators or policies implemented with convolutional layers) on MinAtar and Atari-like games, applying IMP and evaluating mask/weights, mask/permuted, permuted/permuted, and random/re-init conditions.
Fig. 9; Fig. 10

Report the empirical observation specific to CNN-based agents: in several CNN experiments (in particular some MinAtar and ALE/Atari-style games such as Asterix and Space Invaders, as noted by the authors), the performance gap between the mask/weights ticket and the mask/permuted baseline is larger than in the MLP experiments — i.e., permuting the preserved initial weights while keeping the mask intact causes a more noticeable drop in performance for these convolutional architectures.
Fig. 9

State the authors' conclusion from these observations: weight initialization information (the preserved initial weight values) contributes more to the lottery-ticket effect for certain CNN-based agents and tasks than it does for MLP agents, indicating that the initialization plays a larger role in the success of tickets for those convolutional architectures and tasks.

Note that the authors present this as an empirical observation rather than a formal proof and provide supplementary figures for several CNN games to support the claim; this is recorded by the authors and is the basis for the conclusion about CNN sensitivity to preserved weight values.
SI figure 10; Fig. 9

Define iterative magnitude pruning, abbreviated IMP, as the procedure used by the authors: train a network for a calibrated number of environment transitions; measure performance by the average return on a set of evaluation episodes; prune the $20\%$ of weights with smallest magnitude globally (across all layers); reset the remaining weights to their preserved initial values; and iterate this train → prune → reset cycle to obtain a sequence of increasingly sparse networks.
Frankle & Carbin (2019); Han et al. (2015)

Define the term "lottery ticket effect" as used by the authors: the performance gap between a sparse network obtained via IMP and a parameter-matched random initialization with a sparsity-matched random pruning mask.

Specify the reinforcement-learning (RL) optimization formulations considered: (a) on-policy policy-gradient methods, instantiated by Proximal Policy Optimization, abbreviated PPO, which is a baseline-corrected policy gradient algorithm using a clipping strategy; and (b) off-policy value-based methods, instantiated by Deep Q-Networks, abbreviated DQN, trained with a double Q-learning loss and prioritized experience replay.
Schulman et al. (2015; 2017); Mnih et al. (2015); Van Hasselt et al. (2016); Schaul et al. (2015)

List the task modalities evaluated by the authors: high-dimensional visual navigation tasks (a Grid/Maze visual navigation task with observations described below), MinAtar / Atari-like games (pixel-based small-scale Atari-style environments), and continuous and discrete low-dimensional control tasks (PyBullet continuous control tasks and classical control tasks such as Cart-Pole and Acrobot).
Fig. 5; Fig. 6; Fig. 7; Fig. 8

State the experimental protocol used to test for winning tickets across these RL settings: apply the IMP procedure to agents trained with the stated RL algorithms (PPO and DQN) and evaluate whether the sparse networks obtained at various sparsity levels maintain performance comparable to their dense counterparts, averaging results across multiple random seeds and reporting mean best performance and one standard deviation as in the figures referenced.
Fig. 4

Report the empirical observation documented by the authors: across the considered high-dimensional visual and control tasks, and for both off-policy (DQN) and on-policy (PPO) algorithms, a positive lottery ticket effect is observed — i.e., sparse networks obtained via IMP retain performance comparable to dense networks up to non-trivial sparsity levels — providing evidence that winning tickets exist in these RL settings.
Fig. 4

Cite supporting summary statements from the authors emphasizing universality: the authors explicitly state that winning tickets are found in both high-dimensional visual and control tasks (continuous/discrete) and that "a positive lottery ticket effect is robustly observed for both off-policy DRL algorithms, including Deep-Q-Networks (DQN) and on-policy policy-gradient methods (PPO)", which is the textual basis for asserting existence across the listed RL algorithms and task modalities.

Define supervised behavioral cloning, abbreviated BC, as the procedure used by the authors: roll out a pre-trained expert policy to collect a static dataset of transitions and train a student policy by minimizing a supervised loss (the KL divergence or cross-entropy between student and teacher policies, or Huber loss on value estimates depending on setup), thereby creating a training regime with a stationary data distribution that avoids the exploration-driven covariate shift present in reinforcement learning.
Rusu et al. (2015); Schmitt et al. (2018)

Explain the experimental comparison setup used to compare BC and RL: for matched network architectures and tasks the authors apply the identical IMP procedure (train → prune $20\%$ globally → reset) to student networks trained by BC and to agents trained by RL (PPO or DQN), track best-performing checkpoints, and evaluate performance as mean best returns across multiple runs to determine the sparsity threshold at which performance degrades for each training paradigm.
Fig. 2

Report the empirical observation made by the authors: for the discrete action-space tasks and the continuous control tasks, agents trained with RL and those trained with supervised cloning start to degrade in performance at different sparsity levels; specifically, the maximal return of agents trained with reinforcement learning begins to drop at significantly earlier stages of the IMP procedure than for agents trained with behavioral cloning.
Fig. 2

Provide the authors' interpretation linking the observation to properties of RL: because RL entails exploration, within-training covariate shift of the data distribution, and a different credit-assignment signal compared to the supervised setting, the RL problem increases the minimal number of parameters required to successfully learn the task; thus, the minimal winning ticket size (the smallest sparse network that maintains performance) is larger for RL-trained agents than for BC-trained agents in the studied tasks.

State the objective: disentangle the contributions to the lottery-ticket effect of (a) the IMP-derived binary mask that selects which connections survive, (b) the preserved initial weight values on the surviving connections, and (c) the layer-wise pruning ratios that arise from global magnitude pruning.

Define the mask/weights condition (the full IMP ticket): retain both the binary mask produced by IMP and the preserved initial weight values on the surviving connections; this is treated as the canonical winning ticket configuration.

Define the mask/permuted baseline: retain the IMP-derived binary mask and the layer-wise pruning ratios, but permute the preserved initial weight values across the remaining connections within each layer, thereby destroying the precise mapping between preserved weights and surviving connections while keeping the same distribution of initial values per layer.
Fig. 1

Define the permuted/permuted baseline: permute both the layer-wise masks (thus altering which individual connections survive while preserving each layer's overall pruning ratio) and permute the preserved initial weights, thereby keeping only the layer-wise pruning ratios intact and removing both precise mask structure and the original weight-to-connection correspondence.

Define the random/re-init baseline: sample random binary masks (discarding the IMP-derived layer-wise pruning ratios) and re-initialize all weights at each IMP iteration, thereby removing mask structure, preserved weights, and layer-wise pruning ratios.

Reference the tabulated summary of these baselines and their retained components as used by the authors to perform controlled counterfactual experiments; note that this baseline set allows attribution of performance differences to the precise binary mask, to preserved initial weight values, and to layer-wise pruning ratios respectively.
Table 1; Fig. 1

Describe the experimental protocol implementing these baselines: after each IMP iteration the authors apply the respective baseline operation (permutation or resampling) when resetting the remaining weights, retrain the network using the same training regimen, and compare performance curves across sparsity levels to infer which component contributes to the winning ticket effect.

Start from the upstream established result that the IMP-derived mask is the principal contributor to the ticket effect for MLP agents (conclusion 4a) and treat that result as known for the subsequent analysis of what the mask does to input representations.

Explain the authors' analytical focus: analyze the sparsified weight matrices between the input and the first hidden layer of MLP agents to determine which input dimensions have all connections pruned (i.e., whole columns of the first linear layer becoming zeroed by the IMP mask), and interpret the functional consequences for the agent's observation processing.

Report the key empirical observation in high-dimensional visual tasks (the MazeGrid visual navigation example): iterative magnitude pruning successively prunes redundant pixels and entire input channels; when visualizing the cumulative absolute weights of the input layer for an IMP-derived DQN agent, the authors find that IMP removes all connections from certain input dimensions to the first hidden layer, effectively deleting those input dimensions from the agent's observation; the visualized observation size in this example is $o_t \in \mathbb{R}^{6\times 10\times 20}$.
Fig. 5

State the functional implication the authors draw from that observation: the pruned input dimensions correspond to observation components that are not task-relevant (for example, object-channel pixels that encode locations the patrolling enemy cannot access), and therefore the IMP-derived input-layer mask implements a compressed, interpretable, task-sufficient representation by eliminating irrelevant sensory dimensions.
Fig. 5

Report the transfer-test experiment the authors performed to validate that the IMP input-layer mask encodes a sufficient input representation: train a new dense network (i.e., with all weights present) but restrict its input to only the input dimensions retained by the IMP-derived input-layer mask; empirically, the dense network trained on the retained subset of input dimensions learns as quickly and reaches final performance comparable to training on the full observation space, demonstrating that the IMP mask identifies a minimal task-relevant input subset that transfers to dense training.
Fig. 5

Provide additional evidence in MinAtar visual experiments: for multiple MinAtar tasks (e.g., Freeway, SpaceInvaders, Breakout) the IMP mask prunes pixels or object-channel rows/columns that are not actionable — e.g., in Freeway the slowest-moving car channel is pruned most, preserving only pixels needed to react in time; in SpaceInvaders all enemy-bullet pixels that are more than one step away are pruned because only near-term proximity matters; these observations show that preserved input features encode physically meaningful actionable quantities such as proximity or velocities.
Fig. 6

Report the findings in low-dimensional continuous control tasks: despite the smaller input dimensionality, IMP still prunes entire input units (columns of the first linear layer) in tasks like Walker2D, Ant, Cart-Pole, and Acrobot; for example, Walker2D can be trained to full performance with only 11 of 22 observation dimensions, Ant requires 22 of 28; in Cart-Pole IMP prunes cart position and velocity while preserving pole angle and angular velocity, consistent with physical invariances; in Acrobot IMP eliminates sine and cosine transforms of angles and preserves angular velocities which suffice for swing-up.
Fig. 7; Fig. 8

Conclude that, as a result of these observations across visual and low-dimensional tasks, IMP frequently prunes entire input units thereby eliminating whole observation dimensions that are not task-relevant, and that the resulting IMP input-layer mask constitutes a compressed, interpretable, task-sufficient representation whose retained input dimensions can be used to train dense agents to comparable learning speed and final performance; the preserved input features correspond to meaningful physical quantities (e.g., actionable proximity, relative velocities, angular velocities) and therefore form minimal task representations discovered by IMP.

Start from the upstream result that IMP discovers minimal, task-sufficient input representations (conclusion 5) and treat that as established prior knowledge for the analysis of initialization effects on mask discovery.

Define the popular initialization schemes referenced by the authors: Kaiming-style initialization (also called He initialization) aims to preserve activation magnitudes across layers for rectified linear unit, abbreviated ReLU, nonlinearities and typically scales initial weights inversely with layer input dimensionality; Xavier initialization (also called Glorot initialization) is an alternative scheme designed to preserve variance in forward and backward passes.
He et al. (2015); Glorot & Bengio (2010)

Explain the layer-dependent mechanism the authors identify: because Kaiming-style initializations scale initial weight magnitudes approximately inversely with the square root of the input dimensionality of a layer, layers that receive high-dimensional inputs (i.e., large input-layer dimensionality) are initialized with systematically smaller weight magnitudes than layers with smaller input dimensionality; since the IMP pruning criterion is global magnitude of weights, this initialization-induced scale difference biases global-magnitude IMP to prune disproportionately many weights from layers with large input dimensionality.

Provide the empirical contrast the authors present: this layer-specific pruning bias is observed with Kaiming initializations but not with Xavier initializations in the authors' experiments, i.e., Xavier-initialized networks avoid the same strong bias toward pruning high-dimensional-input layers.
Fig. 8

Report the concrete initialization intervention the authors evaluate: multiply the input-layer initial weights obtained from a Kaiming initialization by a factor of $0.1$ (i.e., downscale input-layer Kaiming initial weights by a factor of $10$) and then run IMP; the authors observe that this downscaling accelerates and stabilizes the discovery of minimal task-relevant input dimensions by IMP, producing a robust separation after few IMP iterations.
Fig. 8

Record the authors' caveat about other rescaling factors: smaller rescaling factors than $0.1$ (i.e., closer to $1$) lead to slower separation of input-relevant and input-irrelevant dimensions, while larger rescaling factors (i.e., much smaller multiplicative values than $0.1$) result in overly aggressive pruning of the input layer; the authors present these observations as empirical and heuristic rather than derived from theory.

Conclude from the mechanism and empirical interventions that the scale induced by common initialization heuristics causes a layer-dependent pruning bias (Kaiming causes the bias; Xavier avoids it), and that empirically downscaling the Kaiming initialization of the input layer by a factor of ten promotes robust and accelerated discovery of minimal task-relevant input dimensions via IMP, whereas other rescaling factors either slow the separation or produce overly aggressive pruning.

open_questions.content: The study explicitly acknowledges several unresolved scientific issues and directions for future work. Quantitatively, the magnitude and sparsity thresholds at which tickets remain performant vary across algorithms, architectures, and tasks, so it remains to be determined under which precise conditions the preserved initial weights (versus the mask) become a dominant contributor to the ticket effect in RL. It is unresolved whether the interpretability and representation-regularization interpretation of the IMP-derived mask generalizes beyond input-layer masks to intermediate and higher-layer masks: the role of pruning in shaping hidden-layer representations and the extent to which intermediate-layer masks encode minimal abstractions is not settled. The contributions of the three distinct RL-specific challenges—exploration, within-training covariate shift (distribution shift), and the nature/quality of the credit-assignment signal—to the increased minimal parameter requirements in RL remain to be disentangled. Methodologically, further systematic studies of layer-specific pruning ratios, normalization schemes, alternative initialization strategies, and pruning entire units of intermediate layers are needed to identify sparser, more efficient, and more interpretable winning tickets. Finally, the work is empirical and lacks a theoretical account of why and when IMP uncovers minimal task representations in RL; developing theoretical foundations for these empirical phenomena is an open direction.

paper.authors: Marc Aurel Vischer | Robert Tjarko Lange | Henning Sprekeler
paper.en_title: On Lottery Tickets and Minimal Task Representations in Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper.zh_title: 关于深度强化学习中的彩票票号与最小任务表示
